_link.title: I can describe qualitatively how current, magnetic field strength, and number of loops each affect the torque of a DC motor

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the torque of a DC motor when the current through the coil is increased?
distractors: The torque decreases
The torque stays the same
The torque drops to zero

toLevel2.stem: Which of the following changes would increase the torque of a DC motor?
toLevel2.answer: Using a stronger external magnetic field
distractors: Reducing the number of loops in the coil
Decreasing the current through the coil
Using a weaker permanent magnet in motor

toLevel2.stem: How does increasing the number of loops in a motor coil affect the force on the coil?
distractors: The force decreases proportionally
The force remains exactly unchanged
The force increases then decreases

toLevel2.stem: Which formula shows why current, field strength, and number of loops all affect the force on a motor coil?
distractors: F = mg
F = ma
F = kx

toLevel2.stem: If the current through a motor coil is doubled, what happens to the torque?
distractors: The torque is halved
The torque quadruples
The torque stays the same

toLevel2.stem: Increasing the {{blank:1}} through the coil increases the force and therefore increases the {{blank:2}}.
A stronger {{blank:1}} field produces a greater force on each side of the coil, resulting in more {{blank:2}}.
Adding more {{blank:1}} to the coil increases the total force because each loop contributes an additional {{blank:2}}.
Increasing the number of loops in a motor coil increases the torque produced.
distractors: False

toLevel2.stem: A weaker magnetic field produces more torque in a DC motor.
distractors: True

toLevel3.stem: Why does increasing the current increase the torque of a DC motor?
toLevel3.answer: Greater current increases the force on each side of the coil, which increases the turning effect
distractors: Greater current makes the permanent magnets stronger inside the motor housing assembly
Greater current reduces friction in the bearings allowing the motor to spin more freely
Greater current increases the mass of the coil which gives it more angular momentum

toLevel3.stem: A motor has 50 loops and produces a certain torque. If the number of loops is reduced to 25 while everything else stays the same, what happens to the torque?
distractors: The torque doubles
The torque stays the same
The torque drops to zero

toLevel3.stem: Why does a stronger magnetic field increase the torque of a DC motor?
toLevel3.answer: A stronger field exerts a greater force on each current-carrying side of the coil
distractors: A stronger field increases the current flowing through the coil of the motor
A stronger field reduces the resistance of the coil wire inside the motor
A stronger field increases the number of effective loops in the motor coil

toLevel3.stem: A motor designer wants to triple the torque. Which combination of changes would achieve this?
toLevel3.answer: Triple the current while keeping field and loops the same
distractors: Triple the resistance of the coil while keeping everything else the same
Reduce the number of loops to one-third of the original value in the coil
Halve both the current and the magnetic field strength simultaneously

toLevel3.stem: Why might increasing the current to gain more torque have practical limitations?
toLevel3.answer: Higher current causes more heating in the coil due to greater resistive losses
distractors: Higher current weakens the permanent magnets used inside the motor housing
Higher current reduces the number of effective loops in the motor coil wire
Higher current causes the magnetic field to reverse its direction periodically

toLevel3.stem: In the formula F = nIlB, which variables can a motor designer change to increase torque?
toLevel3.answer: n, I, and B can all be changed by design choices
distractors: Only I can be changed; n and B are fixed by physics
Only B can be changed; n and I are fixed by the power supply
Only n can be changed; I and B cannot be modified at all

toLevel3.stem: Doubling the number of loops {{blank:1}} the force on the coil, which {{blank:2}} the torque.
Increasing the current in a motor increases the {{blank:1}} but also increases {{blank:2}} losses in the coil.
The three design variables that affect motor torque are current, magnetic field {{blank:1}}, and number of {{blank:2}}.
Doubling both the current and the number of loops would quadruple the torque.
distractors: False

toLevel4.stem: A motor with 100 loops carrying 2.0 A in a 0.15 T field produces a certain torque. If the loops are reduced to 50 but the current is increased to 4.0 A, what happens to the torque?
toLevel4.answer: The torque remains the same because nI is unchanged
distractors: The torque doubles because the current has been doubled
The torque halves because the number of loops was halved
The torque quadruples because current has a squared effect

toLevel4.stem: A student needs a motor with more torque but cannot change the power supply voltage. Which modification would be most effective?
toLevel4.answer: Use stronger permanent magnets to increase the field strength
distractors: Use thinner wire to reduce the mass of the coil in the motor
Reduce the number of loops to decrease the coil's resistance
Make the coil from a material with higher electrical resistance

toLevel4.stem: A motor operates at 3.0 A with 20 loops in a 0.10 T field. The motor is redesigned with 40 loops but the field is halved to 0.050 T. How does the torque compare?
toLevel4.answer: The torque is the same because nB is unchanged
distractors: The torque doubles because the loops were doubled
The torque halves because the field was halved
The torque quadruples due to the combined changes

toLevel4.stem: An engineer wants to increase motor torque by 50%. The current cannot be changed. If the field strength is increased by 25%, by what factor must the number of loops change?
toLevel4.answer: The number of loops must increase by a factor of 1.2
distractors: The number of loops must double to compensate fully
The number of loops must increase by a factor of 1.5
The number of loops can remain the same as before

toLevel4.stem: Adding more loops to a motor coil increases both the force and the coil's electrical resistance. What practical trade-off does this create?
toLevel4.answer: More loops increase torque but may reduce current if the voltage supply is fixed
distractors: More loops decrease torque because the increased resistance weakens the field
More loops have no practical effect because resistance does not affect motor performance
More loops increase current because resistance and current are directly proportional

toLevel4.stem: Two motors have the same torque output. Motor A uses 1.0 A with 200 loops, while Motor B uses 4.0 A with 50 loops. Which motor is likely to have greater heat losses?
toLevel4.answer: Motor B, because heat loss depends on I²R and it carries four times the current
distractors: Motor A, because it has four times as many loops generating more friction
Both motors have identical heat losses because they produce the same torque
Motor B, because fewer loops means higher magnetic field strength and more heat

toLevel4.stem: A student argues that making the coil longer (increasing l in F = nIlB) is just as effective as adding more loops for increasing torque. Is this correct?
toLevel4.answer: Increasing l increases the force but does not increase the lever arm, so the effect on torque depends on geometry
distractors: Yes; increasing l and increasing n have exactly the same effect on both force and torque
No; increasing l has no effect on force because l is not in the torque formula at all
Yes; increasing l doubles both the force and the torque regardless of the motor geometry

toLevel4.stem: If the number of loops is tripled and the current is halved, the net effect on force is a factor of {{blank:1}}, meaning the torque is {{blank:2}}.
Adding more loops increases resistance, which at fixed voltage {{blank:1}} the current, partially {{blank:2}} the benefit of extra loops.
Heat loss in a motor coil is proportional to {{blank:1}} squared, so using more loops at lower current can reduce {{blank:2}} losses.

toLevel5.stem: A motor designer must choose between using stronger magnets (more expensive) or more loops of wire (heavier coil). Analyse which trade-offs are most important for a lightweight portable device.
toLevel5.answer: Stronger magnets are preferable because they achieve high torque without adding coil mass
distractors: More loops are preferable because wire is always lighter than permanent magnet material
The choice does not matter because both approaches produce exactly the same motor mass
Neither approach works for portable devices because DC motors are too heavy in all cases

toLevel5.stem: Evaluate why simply increasing the current is not always the best strategy for increasing motor torque in battery-powered devices.
toLevel5.answer: Higher current drains the battery faster and increases I²R heat losses in the coil
distractors: Higher current has no effect on torque so it would be a completely pointless change
Higher current demagnetises the permanent magnets making the motor weaker over time
Higher current is always the best strategy because batteries can supply unlimited current

toLevel5.stem: Compare two design strategies for doubling motor torque: (A) double the current, or (B) double the number of loops. Which produces less wasted energy?
toLevel5.answer: Strategy B, because doubling loops doubles torque without increasing I²R losses as much as doubling current
distractors: Strategy A, because doubling current is simpler and always wastes less electrical energy
Both strategies waste exactly the same amount of energy because they produce the same torque
Strategy B, because doubling loops eliminates all electrical resistance in the motor coil

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that a motor with very many thin loops of wire would be superior to one with fewer thick loops. Critically assess this suggestion.
toLevel5.answer: Many thin loops increase resistance significantly, which at fixed voltage reduces current and may limit the torque gain
distractors: Many thin loops are always superior because more loops always means proportionally more torque
Many thin loops have no disadvantage because the total wire cross-section remains the same
Many thin loops produce weaker magnetic fields because thin wire carries less magnetic flux

toLevel5.stem: Analyse the relationship between the three torque variables and the overall efficiency of a DC motor. Which statement is most accurate?
toLevel5.answer: Increasing B is most efficient because it increases torque without increasing electrical losses in the coil
distractors: Increasing I is most efficient because current directly converts to mechanical energy output
Increasing n is most efficient because adding loops does not affect the motor's power input
All three variables affect torque equally and have identical impacts on motor efficiency

toLevel5.stem: A motor has n = 100 loops, I = 2.0 A, and B = 0.20 T. The designer can increase any one variable by 20%. Which change gives the greatest torque increase while minimising additional energy losses?
toLevel5.answer: Increase B by 20%, as this increases torque without increasing current or resistance
distractors: Increase I by 20%, as this is the simplest change to implement in the motor design
Increase n by 20%, as more loops always produces the least amount of wasted energy
All three changes produce the same torque increase and the same additional energy losses

toLevel5.stem: Predict what would happen to a motor's performance if the number of loops, current, and field strength were all doubled simultaneously.
toLevel5.answer: The torque would increase by a factor of eight because all three variables multiply together
distractors: The torque would increase by a factor of six because the variables add rather than multiply
The torque would increase by a factor of two because only one variable can dominate
The torque would increase by a factor of four because only two variables are independent

toLevel5.stem: Why do high-performance motors often use rare-earth magnets despite their high cost?
toLevel5.answer: Rare-earth magnets provide very strong fields, allowing high torque with fewer loops and lower current
distractors: Rare-earth magnets are lighter than all other magnet types so they reduce motor weight only
Rare-earth magnets eliminate the need for a commutator which simplifies the motor design
Rare-earth magnets generate their own current which reduces the external power requirement

toLevel5.stem: Increasing magnetic field strength is the most {{blank:1}} way to boost torque because it does not increase {{blank:2}} losses.
Doubling all three variables (n, I, B) simultaneously increases the torque by a factor of {{blank:1}}, but the electrical power consumption increases by more than a factor of {{blank:2}}.
